claims.claim: Before reusable boosters, established launch vehicles carried per-kilogram costs to LEO around ten thousand dollars or far more (Space Shuttle ~$54,500/kg; Ariane 5G ~$9,167/kg).
claims.episode_span: every kilogram delivered to low Earth orbit carried an amortized cost on the order of ten thousand dollars or more
claims.supporting_quote: Launch vehicle estimated payload cost per kg Launch Vehicle Payload cost per kg Vanguard $1,000,000 [ 20 ] Space Shuttle $54,500 [ 20 ] Electron $19,039 [ 21 ] [ 22 ] Ariane 5G $9,167 [ 20 ] Long March 3B $4,412 [ 20 ] Proton $4,320 [ 20 ] Falcon 9 $2,720 [ 23 ]

claims.claim: Falcon 9's estimated payload cost is in the low thousands of dollars per kilogram to LEO (~$2,720/kg).
claims.episode_span: Falcon 9 flights now achieve costs per kilogram to low Earth orbit reported in the low thousands of dollars when averaged across many reuses
claims.supporting_quote: Long March 3B $4,412 [ 20 ] Proton $4,320 [ 20 ] Falcon 9 $2,720 [ 23 ] Falcon Heavy $1,500 [ 24 ]

claims.claim: Falcon 9 boosters land vertically and refly - the first landing was on flight 20 in December 2015, and individual boosters have since flown dozens of times (record 37 flights).
claims.episode_span: Today the same booster returns, lands, and flies again, sometimes more than a dozen times
claims.supporting_quote: The booster is capable of landing vertically to facilitate reuse, a feat which was first achieved on flight 20 in December 2015.

claims.claim: Individual Falcon 9 boosters have flown as many as 37 flights, with 598 successful booster landings as of August 2026.
claims.episode_span: Today the same booster returns, lands, and flies again, sometimes more than a dozen times, turning the dominant cost item from fabrication into inspection and refurbishment.
claims.supporting_quote: SpaceX has successfully landed Falcon 9 boosters 598 times. [ e ] Individual boosters have flown as many as 37 flights.

claims.claim: Falcon 9 (Full Thrust) delivers 22,800 kg to LEO expended and 17,500 kg with drone-ship landing - i.e. roughly twenty tonnes of payload.
claims.episode_span: The physics floor is set by the energy needed to accelerate roughly twenty tonnes of payload
claims.supporting_quote: Mass FT : 22,800 kg (50,300 lb) [ 1 ] when expended, 17,500 kg (38,600 lb) [ 5 ] when landing on drone ship

claims.claim: The Falcon 9 first stage carries several hundred tonnes of propellant (395,700 kg) against an empty mass of 25,600 kg.
claims.episode_span: the structural mass needed to contain several hundred tonnes of propellant
claims.supporting_quote: Empty mass 25,600 kg / 56,423 lb Propellant mass 395,700 kg/ 872,369 lb

claims.claim: Recoverable Falcon 9 boosters carry four extensible landing legs and deployable grid fins as recovery hardware; deliberately expended boosters fly without them.
claims.episode_span: Grid fins and landing legs were added as reusable elements whose mass penalty was accepted
claims.supporting_quote: Boosters that will be deliberately expended do not have legs or fins. Recoverable boosters include four extensible landing legs attached around the base. [ 68 ] To control the core's descent through the atmosphere, SpaceX uses grid fins that deploy from the vehicle

claims.claim: Falcon 9 tanks are built from aluminum-lithium alloy (aluminum lithium skin with aluminum domes).
claims.episode_span: aluminum-lithium tanks, Merlin engines, avionics, wiring, and thermal protection
claims.supporting_quote: Structure type LOX tank: monocoque Fuel tank: skin and stringer Structure material Aluminum lithium skin; aluminum domes

claims.claim: On Dec. 21, 2015 SpaceX landed a Falcon 9 first stage — history's first rocket landing during an orbital launch.
claims.episode_span: Today the same booster returns, lands, and flies again
claims.source_title: Wow! SpaceX Lands Orbital Rocket Successfully in Historic First - Space.com
claims.supporting_quote: brought the first stage of its Falcon 9 rocket back to Earth for a soft touchdown tonight (Dec. 21), pulling off history's first-ever rocket landing during an orbital launch.

claims.claim: Per Musk (Aug 2020), booster recovery and refurbishment costs less than 10% of a new booster's price, with a payload reduction below 40%.
claims.episode_span: the marginal expense of a second flight fell far below the cost of building a fresh stage
claims.source_title: SpaceX reusable launch system development program - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: In August 2020, Musk tweeted that refurbishment and reuse of a booster is done for less than 10% the price of a new booster while the payload reduction is below 40%.

claims.claim: Reusability costs payload: the extra propellant and landing gear carried on the first stage cut maximum payload to orbit by around 30% versus an expendable Falcon 9.
claims.episode_span: The approach also trades some payload performance for the propellant margin needed to return the booster
claims.source_title: SpaceX reusable launch system development program - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: extra propellant and landing gear must be carried on the first stage, requiring around a 30 percent reduction of the maximum payload to orbit in comparison with the expendable Falcon 9.

claims.claim: Hypersonic grid fins were added to the booster in 2014 to enable precision landing.
claims.episode_span: Grid fins and landing legs were added as reusable elements whose mass penalty was accepted
claims.source_title: SpaceX reusable launch system development program - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: Hypersonic grid fins were added to the booster test vehicle design beginning on the fifth ocean controlled-descent test flight in 2014 in order to enable precision landing.

claims.claim: Musk's own statement of the reuse economics: payload reduction under 40%, recovery and refurbishment under 10% of cost, roughly break-even at two flights and ahead at three.
claims.episode_span: Because each of these steps attacked the refurbishment cost directly, the marginal expense of a second flight fell far below the cost of building a fresh stage
claims.source_title: How much does it cost to launch a reused Falcon 9? Elon Musk explains why reusability is worth it – ElonX.net
claims.supporting_quote: Payload reduction due to reusability of booster & fairing is <40% for F9 & recovery & refurb is <10%, so you’re roughly even with 2 flights, definitely ahead with 3
